title: Disagreeing with love
hook: streams disagree on practice, conversion and marriage, and still share one people

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: shared ethics. Giving, kindness and justice, from texts the streams read together. What did you give, and to whom? Today, the harder half: what happens when they don't agree. Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

Two schools of teachers, the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, and they disagree. Not once. Over and over, on law after law. In the Talmud's telling, each house insisted the law followed them, and the argument would not end. Then a voice came from heaven and settled it. But listen to how it settled it. The voice did not say one side was right and the other wrong. It said something stranger, and the rabbis kept the sentence. That sentence is where today begins.
screen: `SHAMMAI AND HILLEL.` → `A VOICE FROM HEAVEN.` → `NOT RIGHT AND WRONG.`

segments.voice: Disagreeing with love. Turn it four ways. First, the voice. In the Talmud's telling, it said: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the House of Hillel. Both views are words of the living God. One still becomes the practice. Second, why Hillel. The Talmud asks that question itself, and answers: because Hillel's students were gentle and humble. They taught Shammai's view along with their own, and even said Shammai's view first. They won the law by the way they held the argument. Third, the test. The Mishnah says a dispute for the sake of heaven will last, and a dispute that isn't, won't. Its example of the first kind is Hillel and Shammai. Its example of the second is Korah and his company, who rose against Moses for power. The question is not whether people argue. It is what the argument is for. Fourth, the families. The two houses disagreed even about laws of marriage, which could have split them into two peoples. Yet the Talmud reports that they did not refrain from marrying into each other's families. They kept trusting one another across the line. Today the streams disagree on real things: how to keep Shabbat, how a person converts, whose conversion counts, which marriages a rabbi will perform. Those disputes can wound, and love does not mean pretending they don't matter. The old model offers something narrower and harder: say the other side's view first, say it well, and keep the families at one table.
screen: `THESE AND THESE.` · `HILLEL: GENTLE, HUMBLE, OTHER VIEW FIRST.` · `A DISPUTE FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN.` · `THEY STILL MARRIED EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `DISAGREE WITH LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: disagree with someone lovingly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you disagree with, about something that matters. Not the worst fight you've ever had: one you can carry for two minutes. Now do what Hillel's students did. Say their view first, silently, in its strongest and fairest form, the way they would say it on a good day. Then say your own, just as fairly. Notice whether anything softens. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer before you let them go. The bell holds the time.
Disagreeing with love. Holding a real dispute for the sake of heaven: stating the other view first and fairly, and staying one family. Today's word.
Your line: disagree with love. Today, in one disagreement, say the other person's view back to them before you give yours, and check you got it right. Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Jewish study is built on recorded disagreement: the Talmud preserves minority views beside the law, and study partners are expected to argue hard while learning each other's reasoning.

fork.setup: you're a student in the House of Hillel. you're sure your school is right, and the House of Shammai is in the room. what do you do?
options: state your view loudly and leave.
teach Shammai's view, and say it first, then your own.
refuse to discuss it with them at all.
fork.reveal: the Talmud says Hillel's students taught both views and said Shammai's first, and that this is why the law follows Hillel.

original.note: Hebrew: these and these are the words of the living God, Eruvin 13b.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving someone means agreeing with them.
what it means: keeping a real dispute, stating the other side first, and staying one family.
what a scholar hears: Eruvin 13b's these and these, and Avot 5:17's test: is the dispute for the sake of heaven?

notes: Eruvin 13b paraphrased: bat kol, 'elu va'elu divrei Elohim chayim, and the halakha follows Beit Hillel'; reasons given (gentle, humble, taught Shammai's words and mentioned them first). The Talmud's mention of the dispute's duration was deliberately left out.
Avot 5:17 numbering varies between editions (5:17 or 5:20); confirm reference.
Yevamot 14b: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not refrain from marrying from one another despite disputes touching marriage law; confirm summary.
Contemporary disagreements (conversion recognition, which marriages a rabbi performs) named in general terms only; confirm fair.
Original-language line spelled with full vocalization; confirm.
Editor pass: removed the invented 'day the argument reached the sky' from the hook; the Eruvin 13b retelling now stays with the Talmud's own account.
